title: The white hawk
hookLine: tradition remembers him with a white hawk and a blue horse

lines: A PAINTING ON A KITCHEN WALL.
A BLUE HORSE, A WHITE HAWK.
cards: Look at a Sikh painting of Guru Gobind Singh, on a kitchen calendar, a gurdwara wall, an old book. Often he's on horseback, and the horse is blue-gray. On his raised, gloved hand sits a white hawk.
Sikh songs call him by those two things: in Punjabi, the one with the white hawk, the rider of the blue horse. A teacher remembered by a bird and a horse. Why?

teach.h: A HAWK ON THE WRIST: SOVEREIGNTY.
teach.b: Start with the plain meaning. In the Guru's world, a trained hawk on the wrist belonged to rulers and nobles; hawking was a royal pastime. So a Guru with a hawk carries himself like a sovereign.

That fits his own writings: a man who writes to an emperor as an equal and calls his followers to stand up straight, unafraid. Some Sikhs read the hawk as saying, without a word, this community bows only to God.

teach.h: WHITE: POWER WITH A CLEAN HEART.
teach.b: The songs dwell on the white, and some Sikhs hear it as purity: power held with a clean heart. The hawk is fierce, it hunts, but it comes back to the glove. Strength that answers to someone.

teach.h: THE BLUE HORSE IN SIKH LIFE.
teach.b: Tradition gives him a blue horse, and the image runs straight into Sikh life. Blue is a color some Khalsa Sikhs wear in their turbans and robes, and the Nihang Sikhs, who keep the old martial ways, are known for it.
Riders on horseback still lead some Sikh processions. Here's the honest line.

teach.h: MEMORIES IN SONG, NOT HIS OWN RECORD.
teach.b: These are memories carried in paintings, songs and stories, not details the Guru records about himself.
Tradition holds them, and Sikhs treasure them. They give a face to an idea: a teacher of the One, mounted and ready, with a wild bird that chooses to come back to his hand.

how: Sikh paintings, calendars and devotional songs show Guru Gobind Singh on a blue horse with a white hawk, and Sikhs call him by these images in song.

o: a sign of the Guru's sovereign, fearless bearing
a messenger bird that carried his letters
a bird the Guru kept only to hunt for food

p: a sign of rulers and nobles

s: the Guru describes his hawk in his own writings
the hawk and horse are carried in paintings, songs and stories, not in his own record.
hunting with hawks was a royal pastime
so a Guru with a hawk carries himself like a sovereign.
blue still shows up in Sikh life today
in Khalsa turbans and robes, and among the Nihang Sikhs.

games.q: you're painting the Tenth Guru for a gurdwara wall. what does tradition put on his raised hand?
games.why: a white hawk, sitting on a gloved hand: a sign of sovereignty, in a bird that comes back.

practice: If there's a window near you, find one bird and follow it as long as it lets you, noticing how it uses the air instead of fighting it, and where it lands.
If no bird is in sight, picture the white hawk leaving the glove, circling and coming back, and if you pray, let Waheguru ride along on each breath.

wordCard.voice: The white hawk. In paintings and songs, Guru Gobind Singh rides a blue horse with a white hawk on his hand: a sovereign bearing, held with a clean heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a hawk. Songs call the Guru the one with the white hawk.

carryVoice: Your line: the hawk and the horse. Tomorrow the road runs south, to a river. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sikh devotional tradition, paintings and dhadi songs of Guru Gobind Singh with the white hawk and the blue horse
